title: The Failure of American Education
html:
I had a strange text exchange recently. It made me reflect on the value of a college education in America: what it’s good for and what it’s not.

The setting of the conversation was a dating app, so I didn’t exactly have high hopes for it. Even so, it was rather disheartening, but not for the reasons you might expect.

The platform allows you to display your political orientation. I don’t identify with any particular political sect and am largely disengaged from politics, so I selected the ‘Other’ option.

I matched with this college girl, and, without any greeting, she asked me something like, “What type of political ‘Other’ are you?”

Trying not to start a war, I explained that I spend most of my time trying to make myself useful and that almost no part of making myself useful requires that I bury myself in politics. I also mentioned I wasn’t fond of Trump, Harris, or any politician in the public eye.

“So did you vote?” she asked.

Her profile made it obvious that she believed anyone who voted for Trump, ie. anyone who “voted against women,” shouldn’t have access to women.

Yikes.

I said yes, but, now feeling a bit feisty, I never told her who I voted for. I’m not a Trump supporter (or a Harris supporter, for that matter), but I didn’t want to give her the satisfaction of saying I didn’t vote for him.

The rest of our conversation consisted, more or less, of her telling me how awful everything Trump-related is, and how people who voted for him are bad.

There was lots of common ground between us. We both expressed our distaste for Trump and how it’s a shame to have someone with Trump’s character representing our country. However, I pushed back on the idea that everything Trump is all bad, including the people who voted for him. Undoubtedly, there are brilliant, well-informed, and well-intentioned people — ‘good’ people — who voted for the man, and people who voted differently should be interested in knowing why.

I tried conveying my qualms with her Trump voters = bad framework, and I even asked her to point out what she thought I was missing. So, naturally, she called me an “ASSHOLE”, told me I was wrong, and unmatched with me.

Classy.

To be fair, I can’t say I’m blameless in eliciting such a strong reaction. After all, I did say it was a bummer that some women who are otherwise sweethearts turn into flaming blue-haired lunatics when discussing politics.

I know I know… it wasn’t the least provocative thing I could have said.

That one’s on me.

Nevertheless, it was shocking to me that she couldn’t think of a plausible explanation for why somebody would vote for Trump other than they’re a bad person.

Where was the empathy?

What was also astonishing was that this woman’s profile wasn’t unique. In my experience, Trump-bashing on profiles is commonplace on dating apps and pervasive among college students. Universities should be embarrassed that the level of thinking many of their students are cultivating is Trump voters = bad. I don’t like the guy. He has many flaws, but he is not without his merits. We must keep both in view.

Universities are magnificent places. They produce some of our most valuable knowledge, attract some of the world’s brightest minds, and create countless opportunities for their students. For many, their degree represents their resilience and personal achievements. What it does not represent is their ability to empathize, as demonstrated by my lovely interlocutor.

In Denmark, one of the happiest countries in the world, empathy is baked into their schooling systems1. In America, it is not, and it shows. Have you been on the internet lately? I understand that political issues are near and dear to our hearts, and discussing them can make us unreasonable and hostile. Still, shouldn’t intelligent, highly educated, individuals be able to conjure up a better mental model of America’s political landscape than Trump voters = bad? I find it bizarre that people can spend a decade and a half in school without ever learning to effectively understand opposing viewpoints. How did we get here? How do we get out of here?

I don’t have answers for you, but, dear reader, I would love to hear your perspective on the matter. Please feel free to leave a comment or send me a DM with your thoughts.

Now, to steal an entire outro from an episode of The Tim Ferriss Show:

“And, until next time, […] thank you for tuning in everybody, and be just a bit kinder than is necessary, not just to others, but also to yourself, as you’re looking forward to the next year. Don’t beat yourself up over last year. Just see if you can plan for, not just a better, but more joyous new year. How can you not just do the important things, but do the joyous things? How can you not just do the hard things, but find ways to make those important things a little less effortful, effortless even? These are all questions worth considering. Thanks, everybody.” — Tim Ferriss

1
